Fireside chat at Sequoia Ascent 2026 from a ~week ago. Some highlights: The first theme I tried to push on is that LLMs are about a lot more than just speeding up what existed before (e.g. coding). Three examples of new horizons: 1. menugen: an app that can be fully engulfed by LLMs, with no classical code needed: input an image, output an image and an LLM can natively do the thing. 2. install .md skills instead of install .sh scripts. Why create a complex Software 1.0 bash script for e.g. installing a piece of software if you can write the installation out in words and say "just show this to your LLM". The LLM is an advanced interpreter of English and can intelligently target installation to your setup, debug everything inline, etc. 3. LLM knowledge bases as an example of something that was *impossible* with classical code because it's computation over unstructured data (knowledge) from arbitrary sources and in arbitrary formats, including simply text articles etc. I pushed on these because in every new paradigm change, the obvious things are always in the realm of speeding up or somehow improving what existed, but here we have examples of functionality that either suddenly perhaps shouldn't even exist (1,2), or was fundamentally not possible before (3). The second (ongoing) theme is trying to explain the pattern of jaggedness in LLMs. How it can be true that a single artifact will simultaneously 1) coherently refactor a 100,000-line code base *and* 2) tell you to walk to the car wash to wash your car. I previously wrote about the source of this as having to do with verifiability of a domain, here I expand on this as having to also do with economics because revenue/TAM dictates what the frontier labs choose to package into training data distributions during RL. You're either in the data distribution (on the rails of the RL circuits) and flying or you're off-roading in the jungle with a machete, in relative terms. Still not 100% satisfied with this, but it's an ongoing struggle to build an accurate model of LLM capabilities if you wish to practically take advantage of their power while avoiding their pitfalls, which brings me to... Last theme is the agent-native economy. The decomposition of products and services into sensors, actuators and logic (split up across all of 1.0/2.0/3.0 computing paradigms), how we can make information maximally legible to LLMs, some words on the quickly emerging agentic engineering and its skill set, related hiring practices, etc., possibly even hints/dreams of fully neural computing handling the vast majority of computation with some help from (classical) CPU coprocessors. Stephanie Zhan (@stephzhan) @karpathy and I are back! At @sequoia AI Ascent 2026. And a lot has changed. Last year, he coined “vibe coding”. This year, he’s never felt more behind as a programmer. The big shift: vibe coding raised the floor. Agentic engineering raises the ceiling. We talk about what it means to build seriously in the agent era. Not just moving faster. Building new things, with new tools, while preserving the parts that still require human taste, judgment, and understanding. Video — https://nitter.net/stephzhan/status/2049518659513852109#m

When I was asked by the American Academy of Arts and Sciences to write an essay on my thoughts on how AI will accelerate Science, I felt honored but also felt that it would require a lot of thoughtfulness and diligence to distill my thoughts on paper. The essay has now been published and I cannot be more thankful to the @americanacad and @GoogleDeepMind teams for their feedback and encouragement during the process. Key reflections from my essay: 🔭 AI is our newest revolutionary lens: Just as the telescope and microscope expanded our physical perception, AI is extending our cognitive reach, allowing us to decipher the immense complexity of the data-universe. 🧬 The rise of "machine intuition": AI is not just a computational engine. By detecting hidden structures across disciplines—from protein folding to extremal combinatorics—it acts as an ultimate bridge, accelerating the interdisciplinary breakthroughs that modern science depends on. 🏗️ From puzzle-solvers to architects of questions: As we transition toward open-ended, agentic AI systems that actively generate novel hypotheses, the burden of reasoning is shifting. We are evolving from being the solvers of intricate puzzles into the architects of profound scientific questions. ✨ Expanding human potential: AI won't replace scientists; it expands what we can imagine and achieve. Just as the telescope didn't make astronomers obsolete, AI is giving us the stars. Read the full essay here: amacad.org/publication/daeda…

Harvard University just voted to limit the number of A grades given in undergraduate classes to about 20% of the class. I’m not in favor of this. It deeply runs counter to how I believe education should be. We should hold a high bar, but also work mightily to support the success of 100% of learners, rather than a fraction. Harvard’s administration took this step — over the objections of a large fraction of the student body — to counter grade inflation. Grade inflation is real: Many universities have been awarding A and B grades to ever larger fractions of students, and this has caused grade point averages (GPAs) to become less useful as signals of student skill. At the same time, we want students to succeed. The heart of the question is the role of educational institutions. Should our goal be: - To help students succeed? - To judge students? Both of these have value. But my focus when working in education is almost entirely helping students succeed. To me, it is clear that many people want to learn, to be empowered, to build skills that let them do new things! This is what we focus on at DeepLearningAI. This philosophy is also why my online courses (going back to my early online Stanford courses on Coursera) permitted an unlimited number of retries for graded assignments. I believe in letting — and even encouraging — someone to redo something until they succeed. This is as opposed to standing in judgement of the fact they didn’t get it right the first time. Further, I want homework assignments to be designed primarily to help people practice and learn, rather than to judge their skill level. This is why I prefer to create “Practice Problems” and “Practice Labs” — questions that, when you think through them, help you to gain practice and reinforce what you know. As opposed to “Assessment Problems” designed primarily to judge skill. But won’t Harvard’s move make GPAs more meaningful and help prospective employers identify strong candidates? Having hired a large number of people from Harvard and other institutions, I can say confidently that GPA is not an important signal. We have screening and interviewing processes that give far more accurate ways to figure out if someone is truly skilled. I do not need a wider spread in applicant GPA scores to figure out who's really good! To be clear, there is also value in assessment. Even though standardized testing is much hated, high-quality tests like the SAT, ACT, GRE, TOEFL, etc. provide objective measures of ability in a domain. I find that most people want to learn and succeed. There are also people who want rigorous assessment (for example, to apply for school admissions), but this is a lesser need, and is not my focus when building educational products. Harvard is often described as an “elite” educational institution. There are two ways to be elite: One option involves limiting enrollments, and then even among admitted students, cap the number of people that do well at 20%. I would rather pursue a different path: Set a high bar and teach elite, cutting-edge skills, but strive relentlessly to help everyone succeed. This way, eliteness is defined not by excluding people but by helping as many people as possible to be excellent. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

New course: Transformers in Practice. You'll get a practical view of how transformer-based LLMs work, so you can reason about their behavior, diagnose problems like slow inference, and make smarter decisions about deployment. This course is built in partnership with @AMD and taught by @realSharonZhou . You'll see how transformers generate text one token at a time, how the model decides which earlier words matter most when predicting the next one, and how techniques like quantization speed up inference on GPUs. This is not a video-only course; interactive visualizations throughout let you play with these concepts and build intuition that sticks. Skills you'll gain: - Understand why LLMs hallucinate, and RAG and chain-of-thought shape what they generate - Look inside the model to see how attention and layers combine to predict the next token - Diagnose inference bottlenecks and learn the techniques that speed up transformers on GPUs Join and understand what's really happening inside your LLMs: deeplearning.ai/courses/tran… Video

The MiniMax M2 series was one of the most widely used open-weight LLM series earlier this year. Now, we got a technical report with some interesting tidbits. I summarized some of them below: 1. Full attention as an anti-trend?: They tried hybrid sliding-window attention variants (like so many others, like Xiaomi MiMo, Laguna, Gemma 4, Arcee, Olmo 3, etc.). But even though there were efficiency gains, they said that the production-quality tradeoffs were not worth it for M2. 2. Linear and sparse attention deployment issues: They found that linear and sparse attention are attractive on paper because they reduce the cost of long-context attention, but they are harder to make work well in a production agent system. In particular, they found that these efficient attention variants may be more fragile when KV-like state or intermediate memory is stored in lower precision. Also, they have worse prefix caching support, which matters a lot when using coding agents (which reuse a lot of the context). 3. Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) are useful: Finally a recent MoE ablation study! It's only on the 2B-active parameter scale, but hey, better than nothing. Concretely, they compare a baseline with 32 experts and top-2 routing against a fine-grained setup with 128 experts and top-8 routing. The fine-grained setup improves MATH from 19.6 to 24.1 and HumanEval from 29.7 to 32.5. That's clearly a win for more fine-grained experts (confirming what the DeepSeek MoE paper reported ~2 years ago). 4. Production traffic from frontier models is a golden data asset. If you can efficiently mine the traces, filter for quality, and fine-tune smaller models on them, you get specialized performance at a fraction of the cost. This helps you build a continual learning flywheel: new traces, better datasets, better student models. One increasingly common flow teams are exploring here is Supervised Fine Tuning via Knowledge Distillation from their Traces Basically, we all use frontier models but they’re expensive. And really we just want them to be good at OUR tasks not EVERY task. These frontier model agents produce tons of good traces that show how to do a task So we can mine our Traces for these examples and use them to teach a smaller model how to do those tasks well The smaller model is way cheaper and faster to run and SFT is how we make sure it can match frontier models perf The important piece here is efficiently identifying which traces we can use to train a smaller model. Tools like online evaluators and running agents to read traces in bulk help build this data asset Our goal is to help every team efficiently mine their traces to improve their agents. SFT is one way to do this, will be posting more of how Production Data also helps you build RL Environments and replay your agent behavior to potentially push past frontier performance We want to help every team extract every last signal from every last agent Trace 🚀

Here is another explanation on what an RLM is They did a similar feature for their web search tool recently nitter.net/NickADobos/status/2023… Nick Dobos (@NickADobos) Claude got a huge hidden update. Holy shit. Before: User prompt -> Claude -> uses tool -> Claude After: User prompt -> Claude -> writes code and logic -> that code uses a tool -> code logic can parse or format results, add conditional logic and use tool multiple times -> Claude This unlocks crazy amounts of complex function calling. For example, say you are querying a database. Previously you would do one query, then Claude would read that result and then query again if needed. Now Claude writes code to call the tool, then that code can handle the result and do different things, like query again, strip or format data, and change what it’s doing based on the tool call result, all before being sent back to Claude. The code, that Claude writes, pre plans how to react to the tool result. This compresses LLM agent loops, because the agent isn’t deciding on the fly, and it doesn’t need to keep asking the LLM to make decisions, instead the LLM pre-bakes potentially hundreds or thousands of decision paths. I would not be surprised if we see eventually 2x-100x improvements or more on agent loop & tool calling efficiency scores from this design. Subtle but absolutely huge change. — https://nitter.net/NickADobos/status/2023861257757925469#m

processed.summary: La semaine a été riche en annonces dans le monde de l'IA, avec notamment des avancées significatives dans la puissance des modèles comme Claude Opus 4.8 et Gemini 3.5 Flash, soulignant une course à l'amélioration continue des capacités. Les développeurs ont été particulièrement gâtés avec de nouvelles fonctionnalités pour faciliter le codage et la création d'applications, tandis que les réflexions sur l'impact de l'IA sur la science et la société continuent de susciter des débats passionnés.

glossaire.definition: Modèle de langage de grande taille, un type d'IA entraîné sur d'énormes quantités de texte pour comprendre et générer du langage humain.
Systèmes d'IA capables de planifier et d'exécuter des tâches de manière autonome pour atteindre un objectif.
Modèles d'IA dont l'architecture et les poids sont publiquement disponibles, permettant à quiconque de les utiliser, les modifier et les déployer.
Langage de balisage utilisé pour structurer et présenter du contenu sur le World Wide Web.
Type de réseau neuronal utilisé pour générer des données réalistes, souvent utilisé pour créer des images et des vidéos.
Processus d'ajustement d'un modèle d'IA pré-entraîné sur des données spécifiques pour améliorer ses performances sur une tâche particulière.

category_summaries.actu: De nombreuses entreprises d'IA ont annoncé des mises à jour majeures de leurs modèles phares (Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash), avec des améliorations notables en termes de vitesse, de capacité de raisonnement et de coût. OpenAI a également présenté des avancées pour ses outils de développement comme Codex, tandis que Google DeepMind élargit ses offres avec des modèles d'image et des outils de cybersécurité.
category_summaries.tips: Des conseils pratiques ont été partagés pour mieux exploiter les LLMs, comme demander des réponses structurées en HTML, utiliser des prompts spécifiques pour le codage, ou exploiter les nouvelles fonctionnalités d'intégration comme Appshots sur Mac. L'importance de comprendre plutôt que de juste penser est aussi soulignée.
category_summaries.idees: Les discussions portent sur l'évolution de l'interaction homme-IA, le potentiel de l'IA à révolutionner la science et la recherche, et les défis liés à sa sécurité et son déploiement. La question de la productivité réelle apportée par l'IA et la nécessité de changer les méthodes de travail plutôt que de simplement accélérer les anciennes sont également au cœur des débats.
category_summaries.outils: Plusieurs nouveaux modèles et outils ont été présentés, tels que Talkie pour explorer la généralisation des LLMs sur des textes anciens, des avancées dans les modèles de langage ouverts (open-weights) et des plateformes comme Perplexity Computer s'intégrant aux applications de bureau. La tendance aux modèles open-source s'affirme avec des contributions significatives.

highlights.text_fr: Pour améliorer la présentation des réponses de votre LLM, demandez-lui de structurer sa réponse en HTML. C'est une étape prometteuse avant d'arriver à des vidéos interactives générées par IA.
highlights.text_original: This works really well btw, at the end of your query ask your LLM to "structure your response as HTML", then view the generated file in your browser. I've also had some success asking the LLM to present its output as slideshows, etc. More generally, imo audio is the human-preferred input to AIs but vision (images/animations/video) is the preferred output from them. Around a ~third of our brains are a massively parallel processor dedicated to vision, it is the 10-lane superhighway of information into brain. As AI improves, I think we'll see a progression that takes advantage: 1) raw text (hard/effortful to read) 2) markdown (bold, italic, headings, tables, a bit easier on the eyes) <-- current default 3) HTML (still procedural with underlying code, but a lot more flexibility on the graphics, layout, even interactivity) <-- early but forming new good default ...4,5,6,... n) interactive neural videos/simulations Imo the extrapolation (though the technology doesn't exist just yet) ends in some kind of interactive videos generated directly by a diffusion neural net. Many open questions as to how exact/procedural "Software 1.0" artifacts (e.g. interactive simulations) may be woven together with neural artifacts (diffusion grids), but generally something in the direction of the recently viral nitter.net/zan2434/status/2046982… There are also improvements necessary and pending at the input. Audio nor text nor video alone are not enough, e.g. I feel a need to point/gesture to things on the screen, similar to all the things you would do with a person physically next to you and your computer screen. TLDR The input/output mind meld between humans and AIs is ongoing and there is a lot of work to do and significant progress to be made, way before jumping all the way into neuralink-esque BCIs and all that. actu.text_fr: Aujourd'hui, nous introduisons Google AI Threat Defense - une solution complète de cybersécurité basée sur l'IA, conçue pour surveiller et arrêter les menaces alimentées par l'IA avant qu'elles n'impactent votre entreprise. Voici comment cela fonctionne : 1. AI Threat Defense utilise notre plateforme de cybersécurité @wiz_io pour analyser et prioriser les applications et systèmes présentant le risque de sécurité le plus élevé. 2. Gemini et d'autres modèles d'IA de pointe peuvent ensuite effectuer de manière autonome une analyse approfondie continue de vos applications - en commençant par celles présentant le risque le plus élevé - pour identifier les vulnérabilités de sécurité. 3. Les capacités de CodeMender - un nouvel agent de réparation logicielle - sont ensuite utilisées pour vérifier et accélérer le patch des vulnérabilités. 4. Et nos agents autonomes @wiz_io testent en continu vos systèmes pour trouver les vulnérabilités inconnues avant les adversaires afin que vous puissiez les corriger avant d'être attaqué. Alors que d'autres fournisseurs de modèles se concentrent sur l'utilisation de l'IA pour trouver et signaler les vulnérabilités, Google AI Threat Defense hiérarchise activement vos risques réels les plus critiques et accélère leur remédiation à l'aide d'une variété de modèles, car aucun modèle unique ne trouve un sur-ensemble des vulnérabilités trouvées par tous les autres modèles. Vidéo
actu.text_original: Today we’re introducing Google AI Threat Defense - a comprehensive AI-powered cybersecurity solution designed to help continuously monitor for and stop AI-powered threats before they can impact your business. Here’s how it works: 1. AI Threat Defense uses our cybersecurity platform @wiz_io to scan and prioritize what applications and systems have the highest security risk. 2. Gemini and other frontier AI models can then autonomously perform continual deep scanning of your applications - starting with those at the highest risk - to identify security vulnerabilities. 3. The capabilities of CodeMender - a new software repair agent - are then used to verify and accelerate the patching of vulnerabilities. 4. And our @wiz_io autonomous agents continuously test your systems to find unknown vulnerabilities before adversaries do so that you can remediate them before you are attacked. While other model providers focus on using AI to find and flag vulnerabilities, Google AI Threat Defense actively prioritizes your most critical real-world risks and accelerates their remediation using a variety of models since no single model finds a superset of the vulnerabilities found by all other models. actu.text_fr: Nouveau cours : Construire des agents IA qui génèrent des images et des vidéos -- une frontière peu explorée. Une clé de la performance est que l'agent évalue sa propre sortie et itère pour améliorer la qualité. Ce cours court est construit avec @googlecloudtech et enseigné par Katie Nguyen et Wafae Bakkali. Vous apprendrez trois techniques d'évaluation et les combinerez dans un agent : un score de similarité image-texte pour vérifier que la sortie correspond au prompt, un juge LLM qui note selon des critères personnalisés comme la cohérence de la marque, et des grilles structurées qui décomposent un prompt en questions vérifiables oui/non comme "le sujet est-il dans le cadre ?" et "le mouvement de caméra correspond-il ?" Compétences que vous acquerrez : - Apprendre l'ingénierie des prompts pour images et vidéos - Construire un agent d'image qui transforme les directives de marque en maquettes d'interface utilisateur - Construire un agent vidéo qui planifie des explicateurs multi-scènes et anime des images de référence avec audio synchronisé Rejoignez-nous et construisez des agents qui créent des images et des vidéos ! deeplearning.ai/courses/ai-a… Vidéo
actu.text_original: New course: Build AI agents that generate images and videos -- an under-explored frontier. A key to performance is having the agent evaluate its own output, and iterate to improve quality. This short course is built together with @googlecloudtech and taught by Katie Nguyen and Wafae Bakkali. You'll learn three evaluation techniques and combine them in an agent: image-text similarity scoring to check the output matches the prompt, an LLM judge that scores against custom criteria like brand consistency, and structured rubrics that break a prompt into verifiable yes/no questions like "is the subject in the frame?" and "does the camera motion match?" Skills you'll gain: - Learn image and video prompt engineering - Build an image agent that turns brand guidelines into UI mockups - Build a video agent that plans multi-scene explainers and animates reference frames with synchronized audio Join and build agents that create images and video! deeplearning.ai/courses/ai-a… Video
actu.decryptage: Un nouveau cours propose d'apprendre à créer des agents IA capables de générer des images et des vidéos, en mettant l'accent sur l'auto-évaluation et l'amélioration continue par l'IA elle-même.

actu.text_fr: Nouveau cours : Transformers en Pratique. Vous obtiendrez une vision pratique du fonctionnement des LLMs basés sur les transformeurs, afin de pouvoir raisonner sur leur comportement, diagnostiquer des problèmes comme l'inférence lente et prendre des décisions plus éclairées concernant le déploiement. Ce cours est construit en partenariat avec @AMD et enseigné par @realSharonZhou. Vous verrez comment les transformeurs génèrent du texte un token à la fois, comment le modèle décide quels mots précédents sont les plus importants lors de la prédiction du suivant, et comment des techniques comme la quantification accélèrent l'inférence sur les GPUs. Ce n'est pas un cours uniquement vidéo ; des visualisations interactives vous permettent de jouer avec ces concepts et de développer une intuition qui reste. Compétences que vous acquerrez : - Comprendre pourquoi les LLMs hallucinent, et comment RAG et la chaîne de pensée façonnent ce qu'ils génèrent - Regarder à l'intérieur du modèle pour voir comment l'attention et les couches se combinent pour prédire le token suivant - Diagnostiquer les goulots d'étranglement de l'inférence et apprendre les techniques qui accélèrent les transformeurs sur les GPUs Rejoignez-nous et comprenez ce qui se passe réellement à l'intérieur de vos LLMs : deeplearning.ai/courses/tran… Vidéo
actu.text_original: New course: Transformers in Practice. You'll get a practical view of how transformer-based LLMs work, so you can reason about their behavior, diagnose problems like slow inference, and make smarter decisions about deployment. This course is built in partnership with @AMD and taught by @realSharonZhou. You'll see how transformers generate text one token at a time, how the model decides which earlier words matter most when predicting the next one, and how techniques like quantization speed up inference on GPUs. This is not a video-only course; interactive visualizations throughout let you play with these concepts and build intuition that sticks. Skills you'll gain: - Understand why LLMs hallucinate, and RAG and chain-of-thought shape what they generate - Look inside the model to see how attention and layers combine to predict the next token - Diagnose inference bottlenecks and learn the techniques that speed up transformers on GPUs Join and understand what's really happening inside your LLMs: deeplearning.ai/courses/tran… Video
actu.decryptage: Un nouveau cours en ligne explique le fonctionnement interne des transformeurs, l'architecture derrière de nombreux grands modèles de langage, de manière pratique et interactive.

actu.text_fr: Voici une autre explication de ce qu'est un RLM Ils ont fait une fonctionnalité similaire pour leur outil de recherche web récemment nitter.net/NickADobos/status/2023… Nick Dobos (@NickADobos) Claude a reçu une énorme mise à jour cachée. Sainte-merde. Avant : Invite utilisateur -> Claude -> utilise l'outil -> Claude Après : Invite utilisateur -> Claude -> écrit du code et de la logique -> ce code utilise un outil -> la logique du code peut analyser ou formater les résultats, ajouter une logique conditionnelle et utiliser l'outil plusieurs fois -> Claude Cela débloque des quantités folles d'appels de fonctions complexes. Par exemple, disons que vous interrogez une base de données. Auparavant, vous feriez une requête, puis Claude lirait ce résultat puis interrogerait à nouveau si nécessaire. Maintenant, Claude écrit du code pour appeler l'outil, puis ce code peut gérer le résultat et faire différentes choses, comme interroger à nouveau, dépouiller ou formater les données, et changer ce qu'il fait en fonction du résultat de l'appel d'outil, tout cela avant d'être renvoyé à Claude. Le code, que Claude écrit, pré-planifie comment réagir au résultat de l'outil. Cela compresse les boucles d'agents LLM, car l'agent ne décide pas à la volée, et il n'a pas besoin de continuer à demander à l'LLM de prendre des décisions, au lieu de cela, l'LLM pré-prépare potentiellement des centaines ou des milliers de chemins de décision. Je ne serais pas surpris si nous voyions éventuellement des améliorations de 2x à 100x ou plus sur les scores d'efficacité des boucles d'agents et d'appels d'outils grâce à cette conception. Changement subtil mais absolument énorme. — https://nitter.net/NickADobos/status/2023861257757925469#m
actu.text_original: Here is another explanation on what an RLM is They did a similar feature for their web search tool recently nitter.net/NickADobos/status/2023… Nick Dobos (@NickADobos) Claude got a huge hidden update. Holy shit. Before: User prompt -> Claude -> uses tool -> Claude After: User prompt -> Claude -> writes code and logic -> that code uses a tool -> code logic can parse or format results, add conditional logic and use tool multiple times -> Claude This unlocks crazy amounts of complex function calling. For example, say you are querying a database. Previously you would do one query, then Claude would read that result and then query again if needed. Now Claude writes code to call the tool, then that code can handle the result and do different things, like query again, strip or format data, and change what it’s doing based on the tool call result, all before being sent back to Claude. The code, that Claude writes, pre plans how to react to the tool result. This compresses LLM agent loops, because the agent isn’t deciding on the fly, and it doesn’t need to keep asking the LLM to make decisions, instead the LLM pre-bakes potentially hundreds or thousands of decision paths. I would not be surprised if we see eventually 2x-100x improvements or more on agent loop & tool calling efficiency scores from this design. Subtle but absolutely huge change. — https://nitter.net/NickADobos/status/2023861257757925469#m
actu.decryptage: Une mise à jour majeure de Claude permet à l'IA d'écrire et d'exécuter du code pour interagir avec des outils, rendant les agents IA beaucoup plus puissants et efficaces pour des tâches complexes.

tips.text_fr: Le trafic de production des modèles de pointe est un atout de données en or. Si vous pouvez extraire efficacement les traces, filtrer la qualité et affiner des modèles plus petits sur ceux-ci, vous obtenez des performances spécialisées à une fraction du coût. Cela vous aide à construire un volant d'apprentissage continu : nouvelles traces, meilleurs ensembles de données, meilleurs modèles étudiants. Un flux de plus en plus courant que les équipes explorent ici est le Fine Tuning Supervisé via la Distillation de Connaissances à partir de leurs Traces. Essentiellement, nous utilisons tous des modèles de pointe mais ils sont chers. Et en réalité, nous voulons juste qu'ils soient bons à NOS tâches, pas à TOUTES les tâches. Ces agents de modèles de pointe produisent des tonnes de bonnes traces qui montrent comment accomplir une tâche. Nous pouvons donc extraire nos Traces pour ces exemples et les utiliser pour enseigner à un modèle plus petit comment accomplir ces tâches correctement. Le modèle plus petit est beaucoup moins cher et plus rapide à exécuter, et SFT est la façon dont nous nous assurons qu'il peut correspondre aux performances des modèles de pointe. La pièce importante ici est l'identification efficace des traces que nous pouvons utiliser pour entraîner un modèle plus petit. Des outils comme les évaluateurs en ligne et l'exécution d'agents pour lire les traces en masse aident à construire cet atout de données. Notre objectif est d'aider chaque équipe à extraire chaque signal de chaque trace d'agent pour améliorer ses agents. SFT est une façon de faire cela, nous publierons plus sur la façon dont les Données de Production vous aident également à construire des Environnements RL et à rejouer le comportement de votre agent pour potentiellement dépasser les performances de pointe. Nous voulons aider chaque équipe à extraire chaque dernier signal de chaque trace d'agent 🚀
tips.text_original: Production traffic from frontier models is a golden data asset. If you can efficiently mine the traces, filter for quality, and fine-tune smaller models on them, you get specialized performance at a fraction of the cost. This helps you build a continual learning flywheel: new traces, better datasets, better student models. One increasingly common flow teams are exploring here is Supervised Fine Tuning via Knowledge Distillation from their Traces Basically, we all use frontier models but they’re expensive. And really we just want them to be good at OUR tasks not EVERY task. These frontier model agents produce tons of good traces that show how to do a task So we can mine our Traces for these examples and use them to teach a smaller model how to do those tasks well The smaller model is way cheaper and faster to run and SFT is how we make sure it can match frontier models perf The important piece here is efficiently identifying which traces we can use to train a smaller model. Tools like online evaluators and running agents to read traces in bulk help build this data asset Our goal is to help every team extract every last signal from every last agent Trace 🚀
tips.decryptage: Cette approche consiste à entraîner des modèles IA plus petits et moins coûteux en utilisant les données générées par des IA plus puissantes, permettant ainsi d'optimiser les performances pour des tâches spécifiques.

tips.text_fr: L'utilisation des modèles open-source (open-weights) est en forte hausse. Si vous utilisez des modèles de pointe coûteux, vous pouvez entraîner des modèles plus petits et moins chers en utilisant leurs traces, pour obtenir des performances spécialisées à moindre coût.
tips.text_original: Production traffic from frontier models is a golden data asset. If you can efficiently mine the traces, filter for quality, and fine-tune smaller models on them, you get specialized performance at a fraction of the cost. This helps you build a continual learning flywheel: new traces, better datasets, better student models. One increasingly common flow teams are exploring here is Supervised Fine Tuning via Knowledge Distillation from their Traces Basically, we all use frontier models but they’re expensive. And really we just want them to be good at OUR tasks not EVERY task. These frontier model agents produce tons of good traces that show how to do a task So we can mine our Traces for these examples and use them to teach a smaller model how to do those tasks well The smaller model is way cheaper and faster to run and SFT is how we make sure it can match frontier models perf The important piece here is efficiently identifying which traces we can use to train a smaller model. Tools like online evaluators and running agents to read traces in bulk help build this data asset Our goal is to help every team extract every last signal from every last agent Trace 🚀
tips.decryptage: Il est possible d'entraîner des modèles IA moins chers et plus rapides en utilisant les données générées par des modèles plus puissants, une technique appelée distillation de connaissances.

idees.text_fr: Lorsque l'Académie Américaine des Arts et des Sciences m'a demandé d'écrire un essai sur mes réflexions sur la façon dont l'IA accélérera la science, je me suis senti honoré mais j'ai aussi senti que cela demanderait beaucoup de réflexion et de diligence pour distiller mes pensées sur papier. L'inflation des notes est réelle : de nombreuses universités ont décerné des notes A et B à une fraction toujours plus grande d'étudiants, et cela a fait que les moyennes générales (GPA) sont devenues moins utiles comme indicateurs des compétences des étudiants. En même temps, nous voulons que les étudiants réussissent. Le cœur de la question est le rôle des institutions éducatives. Notre objectif devrait-il être : - Aider les étudiants à réussir ? - Juger les étudiants ? Les deux ont de la valeur. Mais mon objectif lorsque je travaille dans l'éducation est presque entièrement d'aider les étudiants à réussir. Pour moi, il est clair que beaucoup de gens veulent apprendre, être responsabilisés, acquérir des compétences qui leur permettent de faire de nouvelles choses ! C'est sur cela que nous nous concentrons chez DeepLearningAI. Cette philosophie est aussi la raison pour laquelle mes cours en ligne (remontant à mes premiers cours en ligne de Stanford sur Coursera) permettaient un nombre illimité de nouvelles tentatives pour les devoirs notés. Je crois qu'il faut laisser – et même encourager – quelqu'un à refaire quelque chose jusqu'à ce qu'il réussisse. C'est à l'opposé de juger le fait qu'il n'ait pas réussi du premier coup. De plus, je veux que les devoirs soient conçus principalement pour aider les gens à pratiquer et à apprendre, plutôt que pour juger leur niveau de compétence. C'est pourquoi je préfère créer des "Problèmes de Pratique" et des "Laboratoires de Pratique" – des questions qui, lorsque vous y réfléchissez, vous aident à pratiquer et à renforcer ce que vous savez. Par opposition aux "Problèmes d'Évaluation" conçus principalement pour juger les compétences. Mais le mouvement de Harvard ne rendra-t-il pas les GPA plus significatifs et n'aidera-t-il pas les employeurs potentiels à identifier les candidats solides ? Ayant embauché un grand nombre de personnes de Harvard et d'autres institutions, je peux dire avec confiance que la GPA n'est pas un indicateur important. Nous avons des processus de sélection et d'entretien qui donnent des moyens beaucoup plus précis de déterminer si quelqu'un est vraiment compétent. Je n'ai pas besoin d'un plus grand écart de scores GPA des candidats pour déterminer qui est vraiment bon ! Pour être clair, il y a aussi de la valeur dans l'évaluation. Même si les tests standardisés sont beaucoup détestés, des tests de haute qualité comme le SAT, ACT, GRE, TOEFL, etc. fournissent des mesures objectives de la capacité dans un domaine. Je trouve que la plupart des gens veulent apprendre et réussir. Il y a aussi des gens qui veulent une évaluation rigoureuse (par exemple, pour postuler à des admissions scolaires), mais c'est un besoin moindre, et ce n'est pas mon objectif lorsque je crée des produits éducatifs. Harvard est souvent décrit comme une institution éducative "d'élite". Il y a deux façons d'être d'élite : Une option implique de limiter les inscriptions, puis même parmi les étudiants admis, de limiter à 20% le nombre de personnes qui réussissent bien. Je préférerais suivre une autre voie : Fixer une barre haute et enseigner des compétences de pointe, mais s'efforcer sans relâche d'aider tout le monde à réussir. idees.text_original: Harvard University just voted to limit the number of A grades given in undergraduate classes to about 20% of the class. I’m not in favor of this. It deeply runs counter to how I believe education should be. We should hold a high bar, but also work mightily to support the success of 100% of learners, rather than a fraction. Harvard’s administration took this step — over the objections of a large fraction of the student body — to counter grade inflation. Grade inflation is real: Many universities have been awarding A and B grades to ever larger fractions of students, and this has caused grade point averages (GPAs) to become less useful as signals of student skill. At the same time, we want students to succeed. The heart of the question is the role of educational institutions. Should our goal be: - To help students succeed? - To judge students? Both of these have value. But my focus when working in education is almost entirely helping students succeed. To me, it is clear that many people want to learn, to be empowered, to build skills that let them do new things! This is what we focus on at DeepLearningAI. This philosophy is also why my online courses (going back to my early online Stanford courses on Coursera) permitted an unlimited number of retries for graded assignments. I believe in letting — and even encouraging — someone to redo something until they succeed. This is as opposed to standing in judgement of the fact they didn’t get it right the first time. Further, I want homework assignments to be designed primarily to help people practice and learn, rather than to judge their skill level. This is why I prefer to create “Practice Problems” and “Practice Labs” — questions that, when you think through them, help you to gain practice and reinforce what you know. As opposed to “Assessment Problems” designed primarily to judge skill. But won’t Harvard’s move make GPAs more meaningful and help prospective employers identify strong candidates? Having hired a large number of people from Harvard and other institutions, I can say confidently that GPA is not an important signal. We have screening and interviewing processes that give far more accurate ways to figure out if someone is truly skilled. I do not need a wider spread in applicant GPA scores to figure out who's really good! To be clear, there is also value in assessment. Even though standardized testing is much hated, high-quality tests like the SAT, ACT, GRE, TOEFL, etc. provide objective measures of ability in a domain. I find that most people want to learn and succeed. There are also people who want rigorous assessment (for example, to apply for school admissions), but this is a lesser need, and is not my focus when building educational products. Harvard is often described as an “elite” educational institution. There are two ways to be elite: One option involves limiting enrollments, and then even among admitted students, cap the number of people that do well at 20%. I would rather pursue a different path: Set a high bar and teach elite, cutting-edge skills, but strive relentlessly to help everyone succeed. This way, eliteness is defined not by excluding people but by helping as many people as possible to be excellent. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

idees.text_original: Fireside chat at Sequoia Ascent 2026 from a ~week ago. Some highlights: The first theme I tried to push on is that LLMs are about a lot more than just speeding up what existed before (e.g. coding). Three examples of new horizons: 1. menugen: an app that can be fully engulfed by LLMs, with no classical code needed: input an image, output an image and an LLM can natively do the thing. 2. install .md skills instead of install .sh scripts. Why create a complex Software 1.0 bash script for e.g. installing a piece of software if you can write the installation out in words and say "just show this to your LLM". The LLM is an advanced interpreter of English and can intelligently target installation to your setup, debug everything inline, etc. 3. LLM knowledge bases as an example of something that was *impossible* with classical code because it's computation over unstructured data (knowledge) from arbitrary sources and in arbitrary formats, including simply text articles etc. I pushed on these because in every new paradigm change, the obvious things are always in the realm of speeding up or somehow improving what existed, but here we have examples of functionality that either suddenly perhaps shouldn't even exist (1,2), or was fundamentally not possible before (3). The second (ongoing) theme is trying to explain the pattern of jaggedness in LLMs. How it can be true that a single artifact will simultaneously 1) coherently refactor a 100,000-line code base *and* 2) tell you to walk to the car wash to wash your car. I previously wrote about the source of this as having to do with verifiability of a domain, here I expand on this as having to also do with economics because revenue/TAM dictates what the frontier labs choose to package into training data distributions during RL. You're either in the data distribution (on the rails of the RL circuits) and flying or you're off-roading in the jungle with a machete, in relative terms. Still not 100% satisfied with this, but it's an ongoing struggle to build an accurate model of LLM capabilities if you wish to practically take advantage of their power while avoiding their pitfalls, which brings me to... Last theme is the agent-native economy. The decomposition of products and services into sensors, actuators and logic (split up across all of 1.0/2.0/3.0 computing paradigms), how we can make information maximally legible to LLMs, some words on the quickly emerging agentic engineering and its skill set, related hiring practices, etc., possibly even hints/dreams of fully neural computing handling the vast majority of computation with some help from (classical) CPU coprocessors. idees.text_original: Harvard University just voted to limit the number of A grades given in undergraduate classes to about 20% of the class. I’m not in favor of this. It deeply runs counter to how I believe education should be. We should hold a high bar, but also work mightily to support the success of 100% of learners, rather than a fraction. Harvard’s administration took this step — over the objections of a large fraction of the student body — to counter grade inflation. Grade inflation is real: Many universities have been awarding A and B grades to ever larger fractions of students, and this has caused grade point averages (GPAs) to become less useful as signals of student skill. At the same time, we want students to succeed. The heart of the question is the role of educational institutions. Should our goal be: - To help students succeed? - To judge students? Both of these have value. But my focus when working in education is almost entirely helping students succeed. To me, it is clear that many people want to learn, to be empowered, to build skills that let them do new things! This is what we focus on at DeepLearningAI. This philosophy is also why my online courses (going back to my early online Stanford courses on Coursera) permitted an unlimited number of retries for graded assignments. I believe in letting — and even encouraging — someone to redo something until they succeed. This is as opposed to standing in judgement of the fact they didn’t get it right the first time. Further, I want homework assignments to be designed primarily to help people practice and learn, rather than to judge their skill level. This is why I prefer to create “Practice Problems” and “Practice Labs” — questions that, when you think through them, help you to gain practice and reinforce what you know. As opposed to “Assessment Problems” designed primarily to judge skill. But won’t Harvard’s move make GPAs more meaningful and help prospective employers identify strong candidates? Having hired a large number of people from Harvard and other institutions, I can say confidently that GPA is not an important signal. We have screening and interviewing processes that give far more accurate ways to figure out if someone is truly skilled. I do not need a wider spread in applicant GPA scores to figure out who's really good! To be clear, there is also value in assessment. Even though standardized testing is much hated, high-quality tests like the SAT, ACT, GRE, TOEFL, etc. provide objective measures of ability in a domain. I find that most people want to learn and succeed. There are also people who want rigorous assessment (for example, to apply for school admissions), but this is a lesser need, and is not my focus when building educational products. Harvard is often described as an “elite” educational institution. There are two ways to be elite: One option involves limiting enrollments, and then even among admitted students, cap the number of people that do well at 20%. I would rather pursue a different path: Set a high bar and teach elite, cutting-edge skills, but strive relentlessly to help everyone succeed. This way, eliteness is defined not by excluding people but by helping as many people as possible to be excellent. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

idees.text_original: Here is another explanation on what an RLM is They did a similar feature for their web search tool recently nitter.net/NickADobos/status/2023… Nick Dobos (@NickADobos) Claude got a huge hidden update. Holy shit. Before: User prompt -> Claude -> uses tool -> Claude After: User prompt -> Claude -> writes code and logic -> that code uses a tool -> code logic can parse or format results, add conditional logic and use tool multiple times -> Claude This unlocks crazy amounts of complex function calling. For example, say you are querying a database. Previously you would do one query, then Claude would read that result and then query again if needed. Now Claude writes code to call the tool, then that code can handle the result and do different things, like query again, strip or format data, and change what it’s doing based on the tool call result, all before being sent back to Claude. The code, that Claude writes, pre plans how to react to the tool result. This compresses LLM agent loops, because the agent isn’t deciding on the fly, and it doesn’t need to keep asking the LLM to make decisions, instead the LLM pre-bakes potentially hundreds or thousands of decision paths. I would not be surprised if we see eventually 2x-100x improvements or more on agent loop & tool calling efficiency scores from this design. Subtle but absolutely huge change. — https://nitter.net/NickADobos/status/2023861257757925469#m
